newsitem.title: UK: No talk yet in OPEC of oil output hikes.
newsitem.headline: No talk yet in OPEC of oil output hikes.

text.p: OPEC members are not rushing to cash in on the unexpected oil price bonanza by increasing the group's oil output, Gulf oil and OPEC sources said on Tuesday.

The sources, representing several OPEC members, said it was too early to talk about the oil cartel increasing its 25.033 million barrel per day (bpd) production ceiling to take advantage of the increased demand for its oil.
"There have been no discussion at all on this matter. It is too early to say what we will do in November," a Gulf source familar with Saudi policy said

Some delegates said heavyweight Saudi Arabia and other large OPEC producers were not keen to open up debate on how to divide any ceiling increase among the 11 members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

"The price simply is not high enough for us to rush to increase the ceiling. We would be opening Pandora's box by raising it. Everyone would be demanding more quota than they could produce," said an OPEC delegate from a non-Gulf member.

This delegate and others said nearly all OPEC members, with the exception of Saudi Arabia the world's largest oil producer, were pumping as much oil as they could with little regard for individual quotas anyway.
"Face it. We are mostly all at capacity anyway. The only thing a higher ceiling would mean is many more Saudi barrels on the market," an OPEC delegate said.
Saudi Arabia has two million barrels a day (bpd) of mothballed spare capacity over its eight million bpd OPEC quota.
Traders said any formal increase in OPEC's ceiling would likely result in a price fall as the market sells oil futures in a bearish "knee-jerk reaction."

"If OPEC were smart, they would just continue to quietly feed the market extra barrels rather than making a big announcement by raising the ceiling," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy risk management at Swiss bank UBS.

When OPEC last met in June, the group moved up its ceiling to 25.033 million to allow just for an additional 800,000 bpd from Iraq which was expected to be exporting crude by now under a United Nations' food-for-oil plan.
Even though the Iraq oil sale has been put on hold following the military confrontation between Iraq and the United States, OPEC production is running about 800,000 bpd over the ceiling.

But strong demand, a delay in Iraqi oil sales and unexpected supply shortfalls from key non-OPEC suppliers like the North Sea and Latin America has led to oil prices much higher than earlier analysts' predictions.
Brent Blend crude futures hit a post-Gulf War high of $24.39 per barrel in London last week on mounting tensions in Iraq.
Though prices since have eased nearly $2.50 from the post Gulf War peak, they are still about $6 above year-ago levels adding unexpected millions to the coffers of oil producing countries.
Some analysts believed that OPEC could take advantage of the price windfall to increase individual quotas -- except for Iraq's -- for the first time since 1993.
But OPEC sources discounted these reports and said Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members have not discussed the possibility of increasing the ceiling.
OPEC ministers next meet on November 27 in Vienna and will discuss production levels for at least the first six months of 1997.
A Gulf source familar with Saudi oil policy said the kingdom expects the oil price to retain its strength until the end of the year at least.
He cited stronger than expected demand, combined with lower than expected increase in non-OPEC oil production and low industrial fuel inventories as the reasoning behind the Saudi bullishness.
"The market is strong and will stay strong. There are a number of fundamental factors at play," the Gulf source said.
